newsitem.title: GERMANY: German budget gap grows even larger -- media.
newsitem.headline: German budget gap grows even larger -- media.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, already under pressure from a growing budget deficit, faces an even wider shortfall than he has admitted because of lower tax revenue, two publications reported at the weekend.

The news weekly Der Spiegel said federal and state tax experts would, when they meet on Thursday and Friday, reveal that 1997 tax revenue was set to fall 9 billion marks ($5.93 billion) to 11 billion marks short of expectations.
Der Spiegel, in an advance release on Saturday from Monday's edition, said Waigel would have to find six billion marks of this from the federal budget.

The weekly Bild am Sonntag, in an article released ahead of publication on Sunday, said 1997 tax revenue would be down three billion marks and that two billion marks would have to come from the federal budget.
Waigel's ministry declined to comment on the report before the experts' tax estimate was published.

But it denied a report in Der Spiegel which said Waigel was planning to bring forward to 1998 the abolition of a number of tax breaks which were intended to be scrapped in 1999 under a wider tax reform including a cut in income tax.

A spokeswoman said there were no immediate plans for cuts in tax breaks beyond those which had been announced in the 1997 draft budget, and that no decisions had been made on the details of the planned tax reform package.
Waigel has already come under heavy attack from the liberal FDP, partners in the ruling coalition.
The FDP, self-styled party of low taxes, was forced two weeks ago to accept that a cut in an income tax surcharge which it had secured for mid-1997 would be put off until 1998.
Even that only covered half of a seven billion mark shortfall for 1997 which Waigel has already admitted to.

The FDP is adamant that it will quit the centre-right coalition if any taxes are raised to finance the budget gap, and Waigel is committed to avoiding new public borrowing in order to fulfil the criteria for an EU single currency in 1999.

This theoretically leaves him with no choice but to order a new round of government spending cuts in departments and ministries which have already seen their 1997 budgets slashed twice. ($1=1.5180 Mark)
